claims.text: A machine-learning-enhanced workflow can replace most expensive ab initio molecular-dynamics sampling.
An accurate interatomic potential can be trained using only a limited or modest set of high-fidelity ab initio data.
The ab initio training data can capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration coupling contributions to free energy.
Combining the MLIP with thermodynamic integration will provide reliable free energies for both solid and liquid phases near fusion.
The MLIP and thermodynamic-integration workflow will cost only a fraction of a full ab initio MD workflow.
Interatomic-potential simulations can be extended to compositionally complex high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method should initially be tested on elemental and binary systems from 0.8 to 1.0 times their melting temperature.
The method can subsequently be extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The MLIP will reproduce the vibrational density of states relevant to solid-liquid free-energy differences.
The MLIP will reproduce anharmonic lattice distortions relevant to solid-liquid free-energy differences.
Vibrational density of states and anharmonic lattice distortions govern the free-energy difference between solid and liquid phases.
Rapid surrogate evaluations can retain anharmonic vibrational effects while replacing direct ab initio MD sampling.
Rapid surrogate evaluations can retain electron-vibration coupling effects while replacing direct ab initio MD sampling.
Retaining these entropy and coupling effects will preserve the fidelity of calculated phase free energies.
Fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic predictions will agree with explicit ab initio MD to within approximately 10–15%.
For multicomponent systems, the workflow will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
The workflow is applicable through high-entropy-alloy complexity when its training set captures the required configurational diversity.
Extreme local disorder or prohibitively rare-event sampling may prevent the workflow from being applicable.
TOR-TILD has been used as a free-energy baseline for elemental and binary systems.
